Fort Lauderdale, Hollywood & Broward 46

  1. Must see · Bars, Breweries & Cocktails · Fort Lauderdale, Hollywood & Broward

    The Mai-Kai

    Since 1956 the grandest surviving mid-century tiki palace in America — reopened late 2024 after a four-year, $20M+ restoration; gardens, fire-dancers and a vintage rum menu.

    Look for Order: Mai-Kai rum barrel & Barrel O' Rum tiki cocktails with the Polynesian show

    3599 N Federal Hwy, Fort Lauderdale, FL

    Recommended by Miami New Times (incl. Best of Miami), Time Out Miami, Visit Lauderdale (Greater Fort Lauderdale CVB), WPLG Local 10

  2. Must see · Fort Lauderdale, Hollywood & Broward

    Bonnet House Museum & Gardens

    The 1920s Caribbean-plantation-style waterfront estate of artists Frederic and Evelyn Bartlett, between the Intracoastal and the beach.

    900 N Birch Rd, Fort Lauderdale, FL

    Recommended by Lonelyplanet, Culturetrip, Wikipedia

  3. Must see · Fort Lauderdale, Hollywood & Broward

    Stranahan House

    Built 1901 as Frank Stranahan's trading post — the oldest surviving structure in Broward County, now a museum.

    335 SE 6th Ave, Fort Lauderdale, FL

    Recommended by Lonelyplanet, Culturetrip, Wikipedia

  4. Must see · Fort Lauderdale, Hollywood & Broward

    Hollywood Beach Broadwalk

    A 2½-mile 1950s-flavoured beachfront promenade of mom-and-pop shops and ice-cream parlours, with free music at the Hollywood Beach Theatre.

    Hollywood Beach Broadwalk, Hollywood, FL

    Recommended by Visit Lauderdale (Greater Fort Lauderdale CVB), Fodor's Travel, Wikipedia

  5. Must see · Fort Lauderdale, Hollywood & Broward

    Hugh Taylor Birch State Park

    180 acres of Old Florida hammock and mangrove between the ocean and the Intracoastal — paddling, trails, picnic lawns.

    3109 E Sunrise Blvd, Fort Lauderdale, FL

    Recommended by Visit Lauderdale (Greater Fort Lauderdale CVB), Fodor's Travel, Wikipedia

  6. Must see · Caribbean — Jamaican, Bahamian, Trini & Puerto Rican · Fort Lauderdale, Hollywood & Broward

    The Katherine

    Chef Timon Balloo's globe-trotting small-plates room — the Fort Lauderdale pick of three separate guides.

    Look for Order: Trini oxtail with Haitian pikliz; heirloom tomatoes in coconut vinaigrette

    723 E Broward Blvd, Fort Lauderdale, FL

    Recommended by Time Out Miami, Miami New Times (incl. Best of Miami), Fodor's Travel

  7. Must see · Fort Lauderdale, Hollywood & Broward

    Seminole Hard Rock Hotel & Casino (Guitar Hotel)

    The Seminole Tribe's 450-foot guitar-shaped hotel tower, casino and Hard Rock Live arena — Broward's most improbable landmark.

    1 Seminole Way, Hollywood, FL

    Recommended by Time Out Miami, Wikipedia

  8. Must see · Fort Lauderdale, Hollywood & Broward

    NSU Art Museum Fort Lauderdale

    Broward's flagship art museum on Las Olas — 7,500+ works incl. the largest US collection of CoBrA art and William Glackens; free first Thursdays.

    Recommended by Visit Lauderdale (Greater Fort Lauderdale CVB), Wikipedia

    Look for Order: Peel-and-eat shrimp, raw oysters and clams

    1536 Cordova Rd, Fort Lauderdale, FL

North Miami, Aventura, Sunny Isles & Miami Gardens 29

  1. Must see · North Miami, Aventura, Sunny Isles & Miami Gardens

    Haulover Beach

    Wide family beach between Bal Harbour and Sunny Isles — kite flying since 1992, a skate park, and a clothing-optional section to the north.

    10800 Collins Ave, Miami Beach, FL

    Recommended by Time Out Miami, Frommer's, Wikipedia

  2. Must see · North Miami, Aventura, Sunny Isles & Miami Gardens

    Ancient Spanish Monastery

    A 12th-century Cistercian cloister from Segovia, bought by William Randolph Hearst, shipped in crates and reassembled in North Miami Beach.

    16711 W Dixie Hwy, North Miami Beach, FL

    Recommended by Greater Miami CVB, Crazytourist, Wikipedia

  3. Must see · North Miami, Aventura, Sunny Isles & Miami Gardens

    Oleta River State Park

    Florida's largest urban park: 1,000+ acres of mangrove estuary with kayaking, paddleboarding and 15 miles of mountain-bike trails.

    Recommended by Greater Miami CVB, Crazytourist, Wikipedia

    Recommended by Wikipedia, Crazytourist

124 sights and 201 places to eat from Fort Lauderdale down through Miami-Dade to Everglades and Biscayne national parks, each traceable to the source that named it. The food runs on what South Florida does best: the Cuban sandwich and a ventanita cafecito, croquetas and pastelitos, stone crab, Haitian griot, Peruvian ceviche, arepas, key lime pie, Redland tropical fruit, and gator and frog legs at the edge of the Glades.

How this guide was made

How the cuisine filters were policed

Every food card names a specific dish — a cuisine label alone doesn’t qualify. The region’s canon comes first: the Cuban sandwich and medianoche, croquetas, pastelitos and the ventanita cafecito, the frita, stone crab, Haitian griot, Peruvian ceviche, arepas, key lime pie, conch, Nicaraguan fritanga, Redland tropical fruit, and gator and frog legs at the Glades edge. A cuisine tag names the kitchen’s own tradition, never one dish it happens to serve.

Web-searched, merit-measured and fact-checked

Every place is traceable to at least two credible sources (or one institutional authority — Michelin, James Beard, the National Park Service) — the Miami Herald, Miami New Times, the Sun Sentinel, Eater Miami, The Infatuation, WLRN, Time Out, the Greater Miami and Fort Lauderdale tourism boards, Florida State Parks, Atlas Obscura and vetted creators — recorded in data/sources.json. Yelp, TripAdvisor and Google ratings never count as a recommender. Every coordinate is verified into data/geocodes.json and every place status-checked.
